t: After the storm: what Strawberry Fields 2026 says about the Australian boutique festival
d: A sold-out weekend on the Murray brought a new quadraphonic stage, a fearlessly eclectic bill and a Friday night storm that put four people in hospital. The festival kept going. Here is what the weekend tells us.
x: Every festival has a plan for the weather. Most never need it. On Friday night at Strawberry Fields, a severe storm rolled across northern Victoria and the Murray River, bringing heavy rain, thunder and lightning to the site at Tocumwal. Four festivalgoers were struck by lightning. All four were taken to hospital, two men to Shepparton and a man and a woman to Deniliquin, and all were later treated and discharged, according to NSW Health and Victoria's health department. Organisers paused the music several times between Friday afternoon and the early hours of Saturday as crowds took shelter, and enacted their severe weather plan. Footage on social media showed parts of the site under water. In a statement, the festival said the injuries were not life-threatening and that the families of those affected had been contacted, and took time to "thank our medical teams, emergency services, and staff for their fast response". By Saturday the worst had passed, the sun came out, and normal programming resumed. That sequence, a frightening night followed by an orderly recovery, is the story of this year's Strawberry Fields. It is also a reminder of the risks that outdoor events in regional Australia now plan around, and of how much audiences rely on a festival being ready for them. A festival that sells itself Strawberry Fields ran from Friday 20 to Sunday 22 November, with an early-entry opening night on the Thursday, on the banks of the Dhungala, the Murray River, on Yorta Yorta Country. It was sold out long before the gates opened. Mixmag Australia reported that 95 per cent of tickets had gone before a single act was announced, and Early Bird tickets disappeared a full year in advance. Demand on that scale forced a change in how the last tickets were sold. This year the festival ran a ballot, with registrations closing on 30 June and the draw on 2 July, which organisers presented as a fairer way to share out a limited supply. It is a sign of the festival's standing that the question is no longer how to sell tickets, but how to ration them. It was not always so. When the festival began in 2009 it drew about 1,000 people, its director Tara Benney told the Cobram Courier in 2023, and by then it was bringing more than $3 million a year into the local economy. The 2022 edition was cancelled because of floods, after earlier delays during the pandemic. This year's storm, in other words, was not the festival's first argument with the river. The new room The headline addition for 2026 was an eighth stage, The Bazaar, built with the local crews In The Moment Radio and Tribe Soundsystem around a 360-degree quadraphonic sound system. Quadraphonic rigs place speakers around the audience rather than in front of it, so sound moves through the space rather than at it. In a festival that prides itself on the intimacy of its rooms, it is a logical step: an invitation to listen as much as to dance. The rest of the map will be familiar to regulars: Wildlands, The Grove, Deep Jungle, The Beach and the Mirage Motel among them. Deep Jungle was programmed to open on Friday with a celebration of ten years of Finding Figaro, and to host a Mixmag ANZ takeover on Saturday. A bill built on curiosity More than 80 acts were billed across eight stages. The international names leaned towards selectors with deep crates rather than festival-circuit hit-makers: Nina Kraviz, Honey Dijon, Gilles Peterson, Greentea Peng, Yīn Yīn and CC:Disco!, alongside Gerd Janson back to back with Marcel Dettmann, Galcher Lustwerk, Gabrielle Kwarteng, Peter Van Hoesen and Pariah. Gilles Peterson's booking carried extra weight: he was billed to return after a cancellation in 2025. The local programme was just as deliberate. Soju Gang, Miss Kaninna, Mikalah Watego, Lauren Hansom, Cherry Chola, Adriana, Jennifer Loveless and Yasmina Sadiki were all on the bill, along with an Ecstatic Mob takeover and Kia back to back with Moopie. t: CORE lands in Melbourne: inside Tomorrowland’s first Australian outing
d: Next Saturday, Tomorrowland’s house and techno offshoot makes its Australian debut at Flemington. The sold-out show is a test of whether a Belgian festival world can travel this far from home, and the lineup suggests it has done its homework.
x: For years Australian fans have asked when Tomorrowland would come. The answer, it turns out, is that it will not, or at least not in the form they imagined. Speaking to Rolling Stone Australia in 2025, the organisers were blunt: "there will be no Tomorrowland festival in Australia." What is coming instead is CORE, and on Saturday 28 November it takes over The Nursery at Flemington Racecourse for nine hours, from 2pm to 11pm. The show is sold out, with a waiting list on CORE's website. For a first visit to a new continent, that is a confident start, and it gives the Belgian brand a useful data point about how far its name now travels. What CORE is CORE is a standalone brand inside the Tomorrowland world, focused on house and techno and staged in immersive, jungle-themed settings. It began as a stage at Tomorrowland in 2017 and has since travelled to Brazil, Tulum and Medellín. In 2026 it has become a touring proposition: Medellín in February, Los Angeles in May, and now Melbourne, the concept's fifth continent and, as Bandwagon put it, its furthest destination from home yet. The appeal of the format is obvious from a promoter's chair. A one-day event inside an existing venue avoids the cost and risk of building a full camping festival, while the production language, all timber, greenery and light, carries the brand's identity wherever it lands. Melbourne is being run by Collective Minds and Framed Agency, with tickets sold through Humanitix, the non-profit platform that gives its booking-fee profits to charitable projects. Three stages, three moods If the Tomorrowland name suggests main-stage spectacle, the bill does not. The main stage opens with Dino Lenny and builds through Bibi Seck to three 90-minute sets from TSHA, Moodymann and Honey Dijon, before Mall Grab and Effy close the night back to back. Moodymann is the booking that best explains what CORE wants to be here: a Detroit original whose sets are as much about soul, disco and attitude as about house. (We wrote about his long relationship with Melbourne last month.) The Mano stage, making only its second appearance after debuting at CORE Los Angeles, is hosted by Atmosphere and leans darker. Noise Mafia and Peterblue open back to back, Daria Kolosova follows, and Kobosil closes. The stage's lineup also lists HiTMiLØW, Lola Voss back to back with Billy Currie, and fumi, the Berlin-based DJ whose fast, multi-deck sets have made her one of the year's quickest risers (our profile is here). The third stage, ORLO, is where Melbourne's own scene gets the floor. Hannah D opens with a two-hour set, Adriana plays back to back with Edd Fisher, then JNETT, before Jennifer Loveless closes. Bandwagon singled out Loveless and JNETT as the Melbourne selectors on a bill otherwise heavy with visitors. A busy fortnight for the same faces Several of CORE's artists are spending the week before in the country. Honey Dijon is on this weekend's Strawberry Fields bill on the Murray River, as are Jennifer Loveless and Adriana, while fumi is listed on the festival's Wildlands stage. For local audiences it makes the last fortnight of November a rare concentration of underground headliners, and for the artists, a chance to read Australian crowds before the bigger room at Flemington. There is also a local giving component. CULTR reports that Framed Agency is directing AUD 30,000 to the Artists for Kids Culture artsbus as part of the event. What to watch For CORE, the questions are about translation. Can a design language born in a Belgian forest feel at home on a Melbourne racecourse in early summer? Will a crowd raised on boutique festivals and club nights take to a global brand? The ticket sales suggest the appetite is there. The lineup suggests the organisers understood that in Australia, credibility is earned with selectors, not spectacle. If you have a ticket, plan for Melbourne's changeable early-summer weather, arrive early for Hannah D's opening set on ORLO, and save some energy for the end

t: fumi and the art of moving fast
d: She taught herself to DJ on a borrowed controller only a few years ago. Now the Boston-raised, Berlin-based DJ plays Berghain and Awakenings, and this week she lands in Australia for four very different rooms.
x: There is a particular kind of quiet that falls over a dance floor when a DJ is moving faster than the crowd expected. Records arrive before the last one has finished making its point; a kick drum from one deck carries a vocal from another; a third track creeps in underneath and changes the colour of the room. For fumi, that controlled acceleration is the whole idea. Her bio describes "fast mixing and multi-deck construction", and her sets treat four decks less as playback machines than as a single instrument. It has taken her a remarkably short time to get here. When she spoke to tmrw magazine this year, she had been DJing for about three and a half years, and touring every weekend for roughly one of them. In that time her name has appeared on bills at Berghain, Awakenings and Creamfields, and this month she arrives in Australia for a run that takes in a riverside festival, a Melbourne theatre, a Sydney club and Tomorrowland's first CORE event on the continent. From Boston to Berlin fumi grew up in a suburb outside Boston and graduated from Boston College in 2021, having studied abroad in Jordan along the way, with a focus on Middle Eastern politics and international studies. She moved to Germany at 22 through a study programme, intending to do social work with refugees. Music was not the plan. "I took the name from my grandmother," she told tmrw, and the alias has stayed close to home even as the bookings have spread across Europe. Berlin, she said, was "the luckiest thing that ever happened to me". The start was humble. A friend lent her a basic controller and she taught herself everything on it. With one other person she started a collective that threw raves, made podcasts and invited artists onto its own label, and that work led to her first club gigs. She credits the city's underground shows, far from the famous doors, with shaping her taste. Speed, groove and a hip hop ear Her sound sits inside the fast, physical wave that has swept through European clubs: hard groove, bounce, hard house, trance and acid, mixed quickly and blended in unexpected ways. But the descriptions of her that recur most often point elsewhere. Her bios cite jazz, R&B and old-school hip hop, and one adds bossa nova, as influences on how she handles rhythm and phrasing. It is the hip hop DJ's sensibility, the cut and the blend, applied to much faster music. One profile captures her as more interested in the tension of the dance than in stylistic purity, which is as good a summary of the new generation as any. The old-school influence is not nostalgia, either. Her ADE biography describes a musical soul that "lies with driving, energetic groove", inspired by older sounds but built for current rooms. The 240 KM/H effect Much of fumi's rise has run alongside 240 KM/H, the crew she is a resident of and which handles her management and bookings. Her ADE bio says her project has grown quickly alongside that team. 240 KM/H began with what Techno Beats Cloud described as a group of kids from Cambrils and Salou, and for 29 August it announced Back Home, an open-air event for 10,000 people in Salou, with fumi billed back to back with Serafina. Her collaborators tell the same story of a tight scene with international reach. She has played back to back and face to face with Cloudy, Serafina and Adrián Mills, and her list of rooms reads like a map of the circuit: Warehouse Project, Verknipt, Teletech, Terminal V, RSO.BERLIN, Amnesia in Ibiza and elrow Town London. A 240 KM/H session for HÖR Berlin in December 2024 remains one of her best-known recorded sets, and she has recorded for the Awakenings podcast. This October at Amsterdam Dance Event she played the Awakenings opening night at the Sugarfactory and DGTL's Novah & Friends at the NDSM warehouse, and hosted her own night with Intercell at the Bajes. Four Australian rooms Her Australian run is a test of range. She is listed on the Wildlands stage at Strawberry Fields, on the Murray River, this weekend. On Satu

t: Juan Atkins, 1962 to 2026: the man who named the future
d: The Detroit producer who gave techno its first records, its first label and its name has died in Mexico City at 64. For four decades he argued that the machines were there to serve the soul.
x: Juan Atkins, the Detroit producer who laid the first foundations of techno and then gave the music its name, died in Mexico City on Saturday 31 October 2026. He was 64. Atkins was found unresponsive in his hotel room before a scheduled performance at YuYu Cine Club and was pronounced dead after being taken to hospital, according to his agency, Greensmith Artists, which confirmed the death the following day. A cause of death has not been reported. It is hard to overstate how much of the electronic music now played in clubs passes, at some point, through a handful of records Atkins made before he was 25. As one half of Cybotron he made 'Alleys Of Your Mind', 'Cosmic Cars' and 'Clear'. As Model 500 he released 'No UFOs' in 1985 on Metroplex, the label he founded that year. And in 1988, when a compilation set out to introduce the new sound of Detroit to the world, his track 'Techno Music' lent the whole movement its name. "Juan was the originator of Techno, a true visionary," wrote Kevin Saunderson, his friend since junior high school, in a tribute on Instagram. A teenager and a synthesiser Atkins was born in Detroit in 1962 and moved to the nearby town of Belleville after his parents separated. At Belleville Junior High he met Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, the two friends with whom his name would be linked for the rest of his life. He played bass in a funk band and loved Parliament-Funkadelic and George Duke, but the decisive purchase came in his teens: a Korg MS-10, a small monophonic synthesiser. Detroit radio supplied the rest. The broadcaster known as The Electrifying Mojo threaded Kraftwerk, Telex, Gary Numan and Giorgio Moroder through his late-night shows, and Atkins listened closely. He also read. Alvin Toffler's Future Shock (1970) and The Third Wave (1980) gave him a vocabulary for what he was hearing. Toffler wrote of "techno rebels", people who master technology rather than being mastered by it, and the phrase stayed with him long enough to become the name of a genre. Cybotron Cybotron began in 1980, pairing Atkins with Richard Davis, who recorded as 3070. The duo's first single, 'Alleys Of Your Mind', appeared in 1981, and their album Enter followed in 1983. Across 'Cosmic Cars' (1982), 'Clear' (1983) and 'Techno City' (1984) they sketched, in a few minutes at a time, the vocabulary of drum machine, sequencer and synthesised bass that club music still speaks. What made the records unusual was not only their machinery but their temperament. Atkins took the cool precision of European electronic pop and gave it the swing of funk, the result of a Black Midwestern teenager answering Düsseldorf from a car-factory city. Critics have spent forty years trying to describe that combination; he simply recorded it. Metroplex, and a name After leaving Cybotron, Atkins went solo as Model 500 and, in 1985, founded Metroplex. The label was more than a vehicle for his own work. It released early music by Saunderson, Eddie Fowlkes and others, and it gave the Detroit sound an address. Saunderson later recalled that it was Atkins who showed him how to finish 'Triangle Of Love', his first record. Model 500's 'No UFOs', backed by 'Night Drive (Thru-Babylon)', arrived that same year. Then, in 1988, 'Techno Music' appeared on the compilation Techno! The New Dance Sound Of Detroit, and the scene had a word it would never shake off. The Berlin connection If Detroit invented techno, Berlin gave it a second home, and Atkins was among the first to make the crossing. In 1992 he joined Moritz von Oswald and Thomas Fehlmann in the project 3MB, whose 'Jazz Is The Teacher' came out on Tresor. Von Oswald engineered his 1995 track 'Starlight', and Tresor went on to release albums under his Infiniti alias and his own name. The partnership with von Oswald later took shape as Borderland. Berlin remembered. In a tribute gathered by the German magazine Groove, Tresor founder Dimitri Hegemann and the club's team recalled that on the final night at the ori

t: The three typefaces this site is set in
d: One for the interface, one for reading and one for the name: the type behind Creators Lab.
x: Creators Lab is set in three typefaces, and each has one job. DM Mono, for almost everything Every label, headline and button on this site is DM Mono, a monospaced family in three weights and three styles designed by Colophon Foundry for DeepMind, with creative direction from the DeepMind team. It is loosely based on DM Sans, with lower contrast, and was added to Google Fonts in April 2020. A monospace makes everything look like a record of something: a lab note, a set time, a catalogue number. That is the mood we wanted. Newsreader, for reading Long articles switch to Newsreader, a serif commissioned by Google Fonts and designed by Hugues Gentile with art direction by Jean-Baptiste Levée at Production Type. It was made for continuous reading on screens, and it comes in optical sizes, so the letters change shape slightly between caption size and display size. It joined Google Fonts in July 2020. Archivo, for the name The CREATORS LAB wordmark is Archivo at its widest and heaviest. Archivo is a grotesque sans by Héctor Gatti and the Omnibus-Type team, originally designed for highlights and headlines and built to work in print and on screen at the same time. We use it nowhere else. Why three One voice for the interface, one for reading and one for the name keeps the site calm. The only colour we add is a single electric blue, #2723F1. Everything else is black, white and grey.

d: How a tool for making stem cells became longevity science’s biggest bet, what it has shown so far, and what could go wrong.
x: Partial reprogramming is an attempt to make old cells behave like young ones without turning them into something else. It borrows a tool from stem cell biology and uses it gently. Where it comes from In 2006 Kazutoshi Takahashi and Shinya Yamanaka showed that four genes, Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc, could turn adult mouse fibroblasts into induced pluripotent stem cells: cells that can become almost any tissue. Full reprogramming like this erases what a cell is. Partial reprogramming tries to stop well before that point. What it is meant to reset Cells carry a layer of chemical marks on their DNA, the epigenome, which helps decide which genes are read. Those marks change with age in ways regular enough to measure. In 2013 Steve Horvath built an epigenetic clock from DNA methylation at 353 sites, trained on about 8,000 samples from 51 tissues and cell types. Reprogramming winds that kind of clock back. The open question is whether winding it back makes tissue work better. The evidence so far In 2016 a team led by Juan Carlos Izpisua Belmonte switched the four factors on in short cycles in mice that age prematurely. The mice showed fewer signs of ageing and lived longer. In 2020 David Sinclair's lab at Harvard used three of the factors, leaving out c-Myc, to reverse vision loss in a mouse model of glaucoma and in old mice. In 2026 the idea reached people. Life Biosciences began a first-in-human safety trial of ER-100, which delivers those three genes into one eye of patients with glaucoma or NAION. We covered the trial in Rewinding the Cell. The money Altos Labs launched in January 2022 with $3 billion committed, one of the largest raises in biotech, and with Yamanaka as an unpaid senior scientific adviser. Retro Biosciences began with $180 million from Sam Altman and works on reprogramming alongside other approaches, and in May 2026 it announced the first close of a new round at a $1.8 billion valuation. What could go wrong The same factors that rejuvenate can also erase identity, and cells that forget what they are can form tumours. That is why most groups switch the factors on briefly, use fewer of them, or look for drugs that do part of the job. No partial reprogramming treatment has yet been proven to work in people.

t: The Creators Lab 01 cover, in detail
d: Four floating islands, a guitarist, a reader and a creature with a mug: a closer look at Joe Taylor’s cover for our first issue.
x: The cover of Creators Lab 01 is by Joe Taylor, the Berlin-based British illustrator and animator. It is a single scene, drawn in his usual thick, even line and flat colour, and it rewards a slow look. Read it from the top The sky fades from lavender at the top to peach and then pale yellow near the ground, like the last ten minutes of a summer evening. Four islands float in it, each with a flat green top and a jagged underside, as if they had been pulled out of the ground like teeth. On the smallest island, near the centre, a tiny figure lies back and reads. To the right, a larger island sprouts long green plants that curl over its edges like tentacles. Lower down, a red-haired figure in a lavender jumper sits on a rock and plays an acoustic guitar, eyes closed. In the foreground, a lavender creature with a long nose and two thin antennae holds a mug in a yellow hand, surrounded by soft green plants. It looks perfectly at home. Why it is the first cover Creators Lab is about people who make things: in a lab, in a studio, behind a pair of turntables. Joe's scene has all three moods in it: someone studying, someone playing, someone simply watching with a warm drink. His animated work, for clients including Apple, Netflix and TED-Ed, rarely sits still. On paper, he gave us a world that does, for a moment. Read our profile of the artist: Joe Taylor's soft, strange worlds.

d: The Berlin animator and illustrator whose soft, strange worlds never quite sit still.
x: Joe Taylor draws the kind of creatures you half remember from a dream: soft-edged, slightly lopsided, cheerfully strange. A British animator and illustrator based in Berlin, he started out as a graphic designer before illustration and animation took over. Much of his work moves. His illustrations loop and morph, so his portfolio never quite sits still. That style has carried him to clients including Apple, Netflix and TED-Ed, and onto Vinyl Moon record jackets, including a gatefold for Space Case with a rotating artwork spinner. He also makes music as J Yerolota, which might explain why so much of his work feels like it has a groove underneath it. With fellow animator Alex Gamsu Jenkins, he made the 2022 video for "For Willow" by the Berlin house producer Moomin. It opens on a barren landscape that slowly comes back to life, greenery creeping over everything until the whole world is lush and strange. For Creators Lab, Joe made the artwork for our first print issue: calm creatures, floating gardens, a cup of something warm. It is a gentle world, and a good one to spend time in.

t: Detroit Dust on a Melbourne Floor
d: Fourteen years after a rare 2012 visit, the Detroit house icon returns for CORE Melbourne and a Sunday session at the Forum.
x: There's a hush that falls over a Moodymann crowd in the first ten minutes. It isn't boredom. It's a room recalibrating. Whatever you came for, Kenny Dixon Jr. won't hand it over on your schedule. Born in Los Angeles and raised in Detroit, he has worked this way for three decades, and the method hasn't moved. It starts with records. He worked at Detroit's Buy-Rite Music before starting his own labels. When he launched KDJ Records in 1994, he released only 12-inch singles and EPs on it. He named one 2007 track "Technologystolemyvinyle", and in 2010 he was still telling a Red Bull Music Academy audience, "I sell vinyl." The city that kept him Melbourne took a while to get him, then kept him. He made a rare visit in April 2012 and came back for Golden Plains in March 2013, on a bill with George Clinton and Parliament Funkadelic and Mulatu Astatke. On Melbourne Cup Eve in 2022 he and Omar S headlined a warehouse party at The Thorn. Last year he played Northcote Theatre twice: in February on a shared bill with Carl Craig and Marcel Dettmann, and in November on his own, to a sold-out room. A city of record shops, community radio and long sets was always going to trust the person holding the records. "I keep Detroit dust under my feet no matter where I'm standing," he said in 2019. Or, as he told Resident Advisor: "I'm coming to bring Detroit to your stage." Melbourne has never been sold an export version of Moodymann, and it keeps asking for more. This November On Saturday 28 November he plays the main stage at CORE Melbourne, as Tomorrowland's CORE brand makes its Australian debut at The Nursery, Flemington Racecourse, on a bill that also includes TSHA and Honey Dijon. It sold out in August. For everyone who missed out, there's Sunday: Moodymann plays Forum Melbourne on 29 November, with special guest TSHA.

d: Twenty years after a Kyoto lab found a way to reset a cell’s clock, the idea has reached its first human patients. Now comes the hard part: proving it works.
x: The treatment arrives the way many eye medicines do, through a fine needle into the eye. What is different is the cargo: three genes that, for the first time in a human being, are meant to make old cells behave as if they were young again. In June, Boston company Life Biosciences dosed the first patient with the therapy, ER-100, in a small safety trial for glaucoma and NAION, a cause of sudden vision loss. It is the first time partial epigenetic reprogramming, one of longevity science's most hyped ideas, has left the animal lab. A reset button in Kyoto The idea began with Shinya Yamanaka. In 2006 his lab at Kyoto University showed that switching on four genes could turn an adult mouse cell back into an embryonic-like stem cell. A year later his team did the same with human skin cells, work that earned him a share of the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The Yamanaka factors work almost too well. Left on in a living animal, they wipe a cell's identity and can trigger tumours. So researchers tried a gentler version: switch the factors on briefly, or use only some of them, so cells shed the chemical marks of age without forgetting their jobs. Harvard geneticist David Sinclair became the idea's loudest champion. In 2020 his lab reported that three of the factors, known as OSK, reversed vision loss in mice with a glaucoma-like condition and in old mice, and helped injured optic nerves regrow. A clean result would mean a reset button found in a Kyoto lab two decades ago had finally been pressed in a person. From mice to people ER-100 pairs those three genes with a safety switch. They turn on only while a patient takes the antibiotic doxycycline, for about eight weeks, and only in one eye. Up to 18 people are due to take part, at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, Columbia University's Harkness Eye Institute in New York, a clinic in Glendale, California and the Charleston Neuroscience Institute in South Carolina. Starting with the eye is deliberate. Before dosing began, Daniel Ives, chief executive of the rejuvenation startup Shift Bioscience, put it plainly to MIT Technology Review: "If it goes wrong, you've still got one left." Sinclair, a co-founder of Life Biosciences, called the trial "the first opportunity to test whether restoring that information can ameliorate human disease." His ambitions reach well beyond eyesight. In January he posted on X that "aging has a relatively simple explanation and is apparently reversible." He plans to enter an oral reprogramming drug, code-named SL-100, in the $101 million XPrize Healthspan competition. "What we're aiming to do is to epigenetically restore the animal and eventually the person," he said. The doubters Not everyone is cheering. Pete Williams, a neurobiologist at the Centre for Eye Research Australia, fears a failure could set back the whole field: "If this goes catastrophically wrong, it might screw us all in the future." The doxycycline switch, built from parts of E. coli and herpes virus genes, has never been tried in humans, so an immune reaction is possible. Sinclair's animal data on his oral drugs is unpublished, and another Harvard team found that its own chemical cocktail either did nothing in mice or was toxic. Critics also cite his record: in 2024 he stepped down as president of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research after claiming a supplement had reversed ageing in dogs. The first answers The first data came sooner than expected. On 8 October, Life Biosciences reported that the first three glaucoma patients had tolerated ER-100 through day 56, that two of the three had improved visual fields, and that the trial's safety board had recommended moving to a higher dose. Three patients in a safety study cannot show that a treatment works, and the trial was not designed to. Its estimated primary completion date is May 2027. What it can settle is a narrow question: can three of Yamanaka's genes be switched on safely inside a human eye? A clean result would not prove t
